analysis.one_liner: Tightens security, recordkeeping, and inspection rules for licensed gun dealers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2025 with 88 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and has had no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require gun dealers to keep their stores secure with safes, alarms, and video monitoring, check their inventory four times a year, report lost or stolen guns, and run background checks on their employees. It would raise dealer license fees, let the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives inspect far more shops each year (hiring 650 new investigators to do it), and let the agency deny or revoke licenses for dealers it finds dangerous or chronically noncompliant. It would also close the legal loophole that lets private sellers advertise firearms online without going through a licensed dealer's background check. Nothing has happened since it was referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who live near or frequent communities affected by gun trafficking and stolen guns: the bill targets the pipeline of guns stolen from dealers or sold through straw purchases and online private-sale loopholes. Police and law enforcement also gain, since the ATF would get far more trace and inspection authority, and honest licensed dealers gain a level playing field against shops that skirt the rules.

how_it_helps.text: Requires gun dealers to physically secure their premises with safes, alarms, and surveillance, responding to a spike in dealer burglaries and robberies that stole thousands of guns into illegal markets [S3].
Requires quarterly inventory checks and immediate reporting of lost or stolen guns to the ATF, so stolen guns are flagged instead of quietly disappearing from the books [S2, S3].

Lets the ATF inspect every dealer at least every five years — and high-risk dealers annually — removing the current one-inspection-per-year limit, and adds up to 650 investigators to do the work [S2, S3].

Lets the ATF deny or revoke a dealer's license when the business endangers public safety or is unlikely to follow the law, and removes the automatic stay that currently lets a revoked dealer keep operating during appeal [S3].
Makes online marketplaces for gun sales get licensed and route every private sale through a licensed dealer's background check [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Licensed gun dealers, importers, and manufacturers pay directly: doubled or tripled license fees, the cost of safes, alarms, surveillance, and quarterly inventory checks, and up to 650 new federal investigators auditing their businesses. A small slice of buyers would face delays, since the bill lets the government report on multiple sales and requires completion of incomplete background checks rather than letting them default through after three business days.

drawbacks.text: Dealers would bear real costs: tripling most license fees, installing surveillance and safes, quarterly inventory checks, and up to 40 ATF inspections a decade — costs that small independent shops are most likely to struggle with, and which could push some out of business [S3].

The bill would let the federal government build searchable electronic databases of dealer records and loosen long-standing restrictions on using firearms trace data, which gun-rights advocates view as a step toward a national registry [S3].

It repeals the 'default proceed' rule that lets a sale go through after three business days when a background check is incomplete, meaning buyers caught in NICS delays would have to wait until the check finishes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For working people, the bill targets real, documented harms — dealer thefts, unchecked trafficking, stalled trace data — and its main costs fall on dealers' security budgets and compliance paperwork rather than on buyers' wallets. The strongest good-faith objections are the fee hikes and compliance costs that could close small dealers (and the underfunded mandate risk), and civil-liberties concerns about expanded federal record databases and inspector access.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House Judiciary Committee when it was introduced in April 2025, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 3, 2025 and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1, S5].
The action history shows no further steps — no committee markup, no floor vote, no Senate action [S5].
All 88 cosponsors are House Democrats, so the bill has no Republican support in a chamber where Republicans hold the majority [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to change anything: gun dealers keep operating under existing rules, and gun-control advocates have gained a bill to organize around.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun dealers, so far — no new rules

against.name: Gun-rights groups and firearms industry trade associations
against.what_they_did: Organized opposition to expanded dealer regulation and ATF authority (no position appears in the congressional record; opposition to this type of bill is well documented publicly).

sides.party_line_note: All 88 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republicans support the bill, and Republicans control the House and the Judiciary Committee where it sits [S4].

industries.note: Dealers face higher fees, security and surveillance mandates, quarterly inventory checks, mandatory employee background checks, and far more frequent inspections — costs that fall hardest on small independent shops. In exchange they get more clarity on enforcement, but many would face real compliance burdens [S3].
Manufacturers must secure premises, keep electronic records, and pay doubled license fees, but they face no direct restrictions on what they sell [S3].

industries.industry: Online gun-sale platforms and private marketplaces
industries.note: New 'facilitator' rules would require marketplaces to be licensed and force private sellers on their platforms to complete transfers through a licensed dealer with a background check, ending the current unlicensed private-sale channel online [S3].

industries.industry: Firearms retailers with strong compliance practices
industries.note: Dealers already following the law gain a competitive edge over shops that skirt recordkeeping and security rules, since the bill raises costs mainly on noncompliant competitors [S3].

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the House Judiciary Committee with no Republican cosponsors while Republicans hold the majority and chair the committee. With no committee action in months and majority-party opposition, the most likely path is that it dies quietly in committee at the end of the Congress, as most gun-regulation bills without committee support do.
